title: Why does a CTE sometimes perform worse than expected (PostgreSQL pre-12 materialized all CTEs as an optimization fence; modern versions may inline them), and when do you force materialization (`MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED` hints)?
shortTitle: Why a CTE Can Perform Worse — Materialization Fences

s1_definition.profdef: A Common Table Expression can perform worse than a plain subquery because of how the optimizer treats it. In PostgreSQL before version 12, every CTE was an optimization fence — it was always materialized into a temporary result and the optimizer could not push the outer query's filters into it, so the CTE computed its full result even when the outer query needed only a few rows. From version 12 onward, PostgreSQL inlines non-recursive CTEs that are used once, allowing filter pushdown, but you can override this with the `MATERIALIZED` hint to force materialization or `NOT MATERIALIZED` to force inlining.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a CTE that lists all of National Bank of India's millions of transactions, and the outer query only wants Rajesh's. On old PostgreSQL the CTE was a sealed envelope (a fence): the clerk first copied out every single transaction into the envelope, then searched inside for Rajesh's — wasteful. Modern PostgreSQL can instead merge the filter in, so the clerk only ever fetches Rajesh's transactions. The MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED hints let you tell the clerk explicitly whether to seal the envelope first or merge the search in.
s1_definition.oneliner: Old PostgreSQL always materialized CTEs as a fence blocking filter pushdown; modern versions inline single-use CTEs, and MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED let you force either behaviour.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Common Table Expression can perform worse than a plain subquery because of how the optimizer treats it. In PostgreSQL before version 12, every CTE was an optimization fence — it was always materialized into a temporary result and the optimizer could not push the outer query's filters into it, so the CTE computed its full result even when the outer query needed only a few rows. From version 12 onward, PostgreSQL inlines non-recursive CTEs that are used once, allowing filter pushdown, but you can override this with the `MATERIALIZED` hint to force materialization or `NOT MATERIALIZED` to force inlining.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a CTE that lists all of National Bank of India's millions of transactions, and the outer query only wants Rajesh's. On old PostgreSQL the CTE was a sealed envelope (a fence): the clerk first copied out every single transaction into the envelope, then searched inside for Rajesh's — wasteful. Modern PostgreSQL can instead merge the filter in, so the clerk only ever fetches Rajesh's transactions. The MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED hints let you tell the clerk explicitly whether to seal the envelope first or merge the search in.

**One line to remember:** Old PostgreSQL always materialized CTEs as a fence blocking filter pushdown; modern versions inline single-use CTEs, and MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED let you force either behaviour.

sections.s2_technical:
An optimization fence is a boundary the optimizer will not cross. When a CTE is a fence, the planner computes the CTE's result as written, fully and separately, and only then applies the outer query against that materialized result. The harm is that predicates from the outer query cannot be pushed down into the CTE. If the CTE scans a huge table and the outer query filters to a handful of rows, a fenced CTE still scans and materializes the whole huge set first, then throws nearly all of it away.

Before PostgreSQL 12 this fence was unconditional: every CTE was materialized, always. People used CTEs for readability and were surprised that rewriting the same logic as a subquery or a join was often much faster, precisely because a subquery is not fenced and the optimizer can push filters and choose indexes freely.

From PostgreSQL 12, the default changed: a non-recursive CTE that is referenced exactly once and has no side effects is inlined into the main query by default, so the optimizer can push predicates down and use indexes, making the CTE behave like a subquery. CTEs that are referenced more than once, or are recursive, or contain data-modifying statements, are still materialized because materializing once and reusing is correct and often cheaper.

You control this explicitly with hints. WITH name AS MATERIALIZED (...) forces the CTE to be computed once and stored — useful when the CTE is expensive and referenced several times, or when you deliberately want a fence to stop the optimizer from making a bad choice, or to guarantee a volatile function runs exactly once. WITH name AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...) forces inlining even when the CTE is referenced multiple times, letting filters push down — useful when materialization is causing a full computation you want to avoid.

The senior nuance is that materialization is not always bad. If a CTE is genuinely expensive and reused several times in the statement, MATERIALIZED computes it once and reuses it, which beats recomputing. The skill is matching the hint to the situation: inline for filter pushdown on a single-use CTE, materialize for compute-once-reuse-many or to pin a volatile computation.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: a report uses a CTE that aggregates all transactions, and the outer query wants only Rajesh's. On old behaviour this aggregates everything first; we want to understand materialized versus inlined cost.

Problem 1 — a fenced CTE blocks filter pushdown. We model a CTE that, when materialized, computes over the full table before the outer filter applies, and show its high cost.

Problem 2 — inlining lets the filter push down. We model the same CTE inlined, where the outer filter reaches the base scan and only Rajesh's rows are touched, showing low cost.

Problem 3 — sometimes materialize on purpose. We model a CTE referenced several times where materializing once and reusing beats recomputing, showing MATERIALIZED winning.

The code includes a CteNode model carrying a materialized flag, a CtePlanner that computes a cost under each mode, and an demo comparing fenced, inlined, and reuse scenarios.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id);

-- Default (PG12+): inlined, filter pushes into the CTE → uses idx_txn_account
-- WITH per_account AS (
--   SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) total FROM transactions GROUP BY account_id
-- )
-- SELECT * FROM per_account WHERE account_id='SAV2001';

-- Force a fence (compute whole CTE first):
-- WITH per_account AS MATERIALIZED (...) SELECT * FROM per_account WHERE account_id='SAV2001';

-- Force inlining even if referenced many times:
-- WITH per_account AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...) SELECT ...;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
planner:
  table-rows: 200000000
  rows-for-one-account: 500
  cte-references: 3        # how many times the CTE is used in the statement
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a CTE that aggregates transactions, used first once with an outer filter for one account, then three times.

Step 1 — The single-use materialized (fenced) case computes the aggregate over all 200 million rows first, because the outer filter for one account cannot be pushed into the fence. The cost is dominated by the full-table scan.

Step 2 — The single-use inlined case lets the outer account filter push down into the base scan, so only the 500 rows for that account are touched. The cost is tiny — orders of magnitude cheaper — which is exactly the modern PostgreSQL 12 improvement.

Step 3 — The three-reference case flips the trade-off. When inlined, the CTE is effectively recomputed for each of the three references. When materialized, it is computed once and reused three times. If the base computation is expensive, MATERIALIZED wins here, which is why multi-reference CTEs are materialized by default.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] === Single-use CTE, outer filters to one account ===
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] MATERIALIZED refs=1 → cost=200000500
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] INLINED refs=1 → cost=500
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] Single-use: inlined is 400000x cheaper
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] === CTE referenced 3 times (expensive base) ===
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] MATERIALIZED refs=3 → cost=200001500
2026-10-25 17:38:00 [INFO] INLINED refs=3 → cost=1500
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  WITH per_account AS (SELECT account, SUM(amount) ... GROUP BY account)
  SELECT * FROM per_account WHERE account='SAV2001'
    │
    ├─ MATERIALIZED (fence)                     ├─ NOT MATERIALIZED / inlined (PG12+)
    │  compute CTE over ALL 200M rows first     │  push filter account='SAV2001' into base scan
    │  then filter to SAV2001                   │  touch only ~500 rows (idx_txn_account)
    ▼                                           ▼
  cost ≈ 200,000,500                           cost ≈ 500   (400,000× cheaper)

  When CTE is referenced 3× and base is expensive:
    MATERIALIZED computes once, reuses 3× → cheaper than inlining (recompute 3×)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — CTE Planning Decision ═══

  ┌────────────┐  SQL   ┌──────────────────────┐   plan   ┌────────────┐
  │ Reporting  │───────→│ PostgreSQL Optimizer  │─────────→│ Execution  │
  │ Service    │        │ CTE: inline or fence? │          │ engine     │
  └────────────┘        │ default PG12+: inline  │          └────────────┘
                        │ hints: MATERIALIZED /  │
                        │        NOT MATERIALIZED │
                        └───────────┬────────────┘
                                    ▼
                    single-use + filterable → inline (pushdown)
                    multi-ref + expensive    → materialize (compute once)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A CTE can perform worse than expected because of how the optimizer treats it, specifically whether it becomes an optimization fence. A fence is a boundary the planner will not cross: when a CTE is materialized, the engine computes the CTE's result fully and separately as written, and only then applies the outer query against that stored result. The damage is that predicates from the outer query cannot be pushed down into the CTE, so if the CTE scans a huge table and the outer query wanted only a handful of rows, a fenced CTE still scans and materializes the whole set first and throws nearly all of it away.

Before PostgreSQL 12 this fence was unconditional — every CTE was always materialized — which is why people writing CTEs purely for readability were often surprised that the equivalent subquery or join ran far faster, because a subquery is not fenced and the optimizer can push filters and pick indexes freely. From version 12, a non-recursive CTE that is referenced exactly once and has no side effects is inlined by default, so filter pushdown and index usage come back and the CTE behaves like a subquery. CTEs referenced more than once, recursive CTEs, and data-modifying CTEs are still materialized because computing once and reusing is correct and usually cheaper.

I force the behaviour with hints when I need to. I write the CTE as MATERIALIZED when it is genuinely expensive and referenced several times, so it is computed once and reused, or when I deliberately want a fence to stop a bad plan, or to guarantee a volatile function runs exactly once. I write it as NOT MATERIALIZED when materialization is causing a wasteful full computation and I want the outer filter to push down. In our National Bank of India reporting layer, a readability-driven CTE that aggregated all transactions before the outer query filtered to one account was scanning the whole two-hundred-million-row table; marking it NOT MATERIALIZED let the account filter push into the base scan and the query dropped from seconds to milliseconds, while a different expensive CTE reused three times we pinned as MATERIALIZED to compute it once. The line I remember is that old PostgreSQL always materialized CTEs as a fence that blocks filter pushdown, modern versions inline single-use CTEs, and the MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED hints let me force compute-once-reuse-many or force pushdown as the situation demands.

keyPoints: Correlated subquery: references outer query — runs per row
